questions.explanation: The log decouples the two sides: producers just append events and each consumer reads at its own pace. Option 0 is wrong because consumers process independently, not simultaneously; option 2 is wrong because consumers still need schemas to interpret events; option 3 describes federated querying, not log-based integration.
options: It guarantees every consumer sees identical data at the same instant
It decouples producers from consumers, so each side can evolve and scale independently
It eliminates the need for any schema or data model in downstream systems
It makes cross-system joins faster than querying the sources directly
questions.question: A company replaces nightly ETL dumps with change-data-capture events published into a durable log that each downstream team consumes independently. What is the main architectural advantage of the log-based approach?

questions.explanation: Batch ETL's staleness and brittleness (0) and the log as a decoupled backbone (1) are the chapter's core contrasts. Option 2 is backwards: federated querying defers joins and consistency to query time rather than solving them upfront. Option 3 is the opposite of the truth — decoupling is the whole point of the log.
options: Batch ETL leaves data stale between runs and tends to break when source schemas change
A single log can serve as the integration backbone, with each consumer reading at its own pace
Federated querying solves cross-system joins and consistency problems once, at integration time
Log-based integration requires all producers and consumers to deploy and scale in lockstep
questions.question: Which statements about data-integration approaches are true?

questions.explanation: The log is the durable system of record; specialized stores (search index, cache, warehouse) are derived from it. Option 0 confuses the log with an ephemeral queue; option 1 is wrong because derived views and indexes still exist — they're just separate tools; option 3 describes data virtualization, not the log's role.
options: It is a temporary buffer that can be discarded once consumers acknowledge messages
It replaces the need for any indexes or materialized views
It serves as the system of record from which specialized derived stores are built
It acts as the query engine that federates reads across the derived stores
questions.question: In an 'unbundled' architecture, what role does the durable event log play?

questions.explanation: Deterministic replay makes derived stores rebuildable (0); Lambda's batch layer corrects the speed layer (1); Kappa reprocesses by replaying the log through one pipeline (3). Option 2 describes Lambda's dual-codebase drawback — Kappa exists precisely to eliminate it with a single stream pipeline.
options: A corrupted or lost derived store can be rebuilt by replaying the log
In the Lambda architecture, the batch layer recomputes over the full dataset and eventually corrects the speed layer's approximations
The Kappa architecture keeps separate batch and speed codebases to maximize reliability
In the Kappa architecture, reprocessing historical data means replaying the log through updated stream jobs
questions.question: Which statements about unbundled architectures are true?

questions.explanation: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits commands that change state from the read-optimized views derived from the resulting events. Option 0 is storage/compute disaggregation; option 2 is the Kappa architecture; option 3 is just backup strategy — none involve the write/read model split.
options: It separates compute from storage so each can scale independently
It separates the write model (commands) from read models (derived views) so each can be optimized for its own access pattern
It separates batch jobs from stream jobs to avoid the Lambda architecture's dual code paths
It separates the system of record from its backups for disaster recovery
questions.question: What does CQRS separate, and why?

questions.explanation: The end-to-end argument: a component-level guarantee (delivery) does not compose into an end-to-end guarantee (effects) — the consumer can crash between applying and acknowledging. Option 3 is the central misconception the chapter attacks; option 2 misdiagnoses a correct broker; option 0 throws away a useful (if insufficient) guarantee.
options: The broker's guarantee is useless and should be replaced with at-least-once delivery
Correctness must hold across the whole pipeline: the consumer's writes must also be idempotent, since delivery guarantees alone don't prevent double-applying
The duplicates prove the broker is misconfigured and violating its own guarantee
Exactly-once delivery automatically makes all downstream effects happen exactly once
questions.question: A message broker guarantees exactly-once delivery to a consumer, yet duplicate charges still appear. What does the end-to-end argument say about this?

questions.explanation: Partitioning the log by the constrained key funnels every claim for a name through one consumer, which can check and reject duplicates authoritatively. Option 0 permits duplicates by design; option 2 moves enforcement to reads, which cannot reject a write; option 3 confuses idempotence (one request applied once) with conflict resolution between different requests.
options: Let every partition accept the name and resolve collisions with last-write-wins
Route all writes for a given username to the same partition so one consumer can authoritatively reject duplicates
Store usernames in each derived view and merge them lazily at read time
Rely on idempotent producers to prevent two users from choosing the same name
questions.question: You must enforce globally unique usernames in a system whose writes flow through a partitioned log. What is the standard approach?

questions.explanation: Deterministic IDs (0), repeat-safe consumer logic (1), and atomic offset commits (3) all make retries safe. Option 2 is the trap: redelivery is only harmless if the consumer is already idempotent — at-least-once delivery by itself guarantees duplicates will be redelivered, not that they'll be harmless.
options: Derive record IDs deterministically from the request or event, so a retry writes the same record instead of a new one
Design the consumer so that processing the same event twice leaves the same resulting state
Rely on at-least-once delivery alone, since redelivery is harmless by definition
Where the store supports it, commit the processed offset atomically with the write
questions.question: Which practices help make a pipeline's effects idempotent?

questions.explanation: Cross-partition atomicity is expensive (0), the outbox pattern is the pragmatic alternative (1), and derived-view staleness must be bounded explicitly (3). Option 2 is the misconception: 2PC is blocking, slow, and operationally heavy — exactly why the chapter steers designs away from needing it.
options: Atomic writes spanning multiple partitions require coordination such as two-phase commit, so designs should avoid needing them where possible
When cross-partition atomicity is unavoidable, patterns like the transactional outbox are preferable to ad-hoc coordination
Two-phase commit is the recommended default for everyday multi-partition writes because it is simple and fast
Derived views always lag the log, so you should state explicitly how stale a view may be and whether that is acceptable
questions.question: Which statements about correctness across partitions and over time are true?

questions.explanation: The loop is self-reinforcing: biased data drives deployment, deployment generates the very incidents the data records, and the model reads that as validation. Option 0 inverts the causality; option 2 wrongly assumes sharing fixes biased labels; option 3 describes adversarial adaptation, a different problem than the bias-amplification loop.
options: More accurate predictions reduce policing, which then makes future predictions less accurate
Biased historical data sends more police to an area, producing more recorded incidents there, which the model treats as confirmation of higher crime
Police departments share data with each other, which averages out local biases over time
Criminals adapt to predicted patrols, so the model's accuracy decays and policing becomes random
questions.question: What feedback loop makes predictive policing a cautionary example in the chapter?

questions.explanation: Fictional consent (0), verifiable auditability (1), and engineers' responsibility for foreseeable consequences (2) are the chapter's three pillars here. Option 3 is doubly wrong: more data can amplify bias through feedback loops (see predictive policing), and the ethical concerns extend well beyond breaches to fairness, surveillance, and secondary use.
options: Consent buried in terms and conditions is rarely informed, so 'the user agreed' is a weak ethical basis for data use
Cryptographic audit logs let outsiders verify what a data controller actually did — trust, but verify
Engineers who build data systems bear responsibility for the foreseeable consequences of those systems
Collecting more data automatically reduces bias, so the ethical concern is only about data breaches
questions.question: Which statements reflect the chapter's discussion of responsibility in data systems?

questions.explanation: The closing synthesis is convergence (batch + stream on the log), end-to-end correctness by design, and ethics as part of engineering. Option 0 contradicts the unbundling thesis; option 2 contradicts the end-to-end argument; option 3 contradicts the entire 'Doing the Right Thing' section.
options: One ever-larger database will eventually re-bundle every feature, making specialized tools obsolete
Batch and stream processing converge around log-centric architectures, with correctness designed end-to-end and ethical responsibility treated as engineering work
Correctness guarantees will move entirely into message brokers, freeing application developers from thinking about idempotence
Ethics is a policy matter for lawyers, not something data-system design needs to address
questions.question: Which best captures the future direction the book's closing chapter sketches?

summary.overview: Chapter 12 ties the whole book together: rather than one database that does everything, future data systems are built around a durable event log that integrates disparate systems, feeds specialized derived stores, and makes end-to-end correctness achievable. It closes by reminding engineers that data systems shape society, so building them well includes an ethical responsibility.

sections.heading: Data Integration
takeaways: Log-based integration (capturing change events into a durable log) decouples producers from consumers: each side evolves and scales independently, and consumers process at their own pace.
Batch ETL (periodic extract-transform-load into a warehouse) is simple to reason about, but data goes stale between runs and pipelines break when source schemas change.
Federated querying presents one query interface over many sources, but it defers hard problems — cross-system joins, performance, consistency — to query time instead of solving them upfront.

sections.heading: Unbundling Databases
takeaways: Unbundling replaces the one-database-that-does-everything with specialized tools: a durable log as the system of record, plus derived stores each optimized for one job (search, caching, analytics).
Because derivation is deterministic, any derived view can be rebuilt from scratch by replaying the log — losing a derived store is an inconvenience, not data loss.

Lambda architecture pairs a batch layer (recomputes over the full dataset: accurate but high-latency) with a speed layer (stream processing over recent data: fast but approximate); the batch layer's results eventually correct the speed layer's.
Kappa architecture drops the two-layer complexity: a single stream-processing pipeline handles everything, and reprocessing just means replaying the log through updated jobs.
CQRS separates the write model (commands that change state) from read models (views derived from the resulting events), so each side can be optimized for its own access pattern.

sections.heading: Aiming for Correctness
takeaways: The end-to-end argument: correctness guarantees must span the whole pipeline — exactly-once delivery by a broker alone does not produce exactly-once effects if the consumer can still double-apply.
Enforce uniqueness (e.g., unique usernames) by routing every write for the constrained key to the same partition, so a single consumer can authoritatively check for duplicates.
Design operations to be idempotent — e.g., derive record IDs deterministically from the request — so that retries after failures cannot create duplicate effects.
Atomic writes spanning multiple partitions need coordination such as two-phase commit; prefer designs that avoid them, or use patterns such as the transactional outbox when they are unavoidable.
Derived views always lag the log, so state explicitly how stale a view may be and whether that staleness is acceptable for the decisions made from it.

sections.heading: Doing the Right Thing
takeaways: Predictive policing illustrates a harmful feedback loop: biased historical data directs more policing to an area, producing more recorded incidents, which the model then treats as confirmation of higher crime.
Consent is often fictional — almost nobody reads terms and conditions — so 'the user agreed' is a weak ethical basis for data collection and secondary uses.
'Trust, but verify': cryptographic audit logs (in the spirit of Certificate Transparency) let outsiders check what a data controller actually did with data.
Engineers who build data systems wield real power over people's lives and therefore bear responsibility for the foreseeable consequences of those systems.

sections.heading: Summary
takeaways: The book's arc closes on three durable concerns — reliability, scalability, maintainability — with the log emerging as the unifying foundation for both operational and analytical data.
The future it sketches: batch and stream processing converge, correctness is designed end-to-end rather than bolted on, and ethical responsibility is treated as part of the engineering job.
